subject: Biology
title: Bacteriophages: Virus vs Bacteria
description: A micro-lesson that makes Bacteriophages: Virus vs Bacteria usable.

hook.text: There are viruses that don't infect us—they infect bacteria. They're called bacteriophages.

buildup.text: Phages look like tiny lunar landers. They inject DNA into bacteria and destroy them from inside.

discovery.text: There are an estimated 10 trillion trillion phages on Earth—more than any other biological entity.

twist.text: Phage therapy could treat antibiotic-resistant infections by sending viruses to kill bacteria.

climax.text: As antibiotic resistance grows, phages are being reconsidered as medicine's next weapon.

punchline.text: The enemy of your enemy might save you.

details.summary: Bacteriophages are viruses that exclusively infect and kill bacteria. They are the most abundant biological entities on Earth, numbering an estimated 10 to the 31st power. Phage therapy, using bacteriophages to treat bacterial infections, is gaining renewed interest as antibiotic resistance grows.
details.whyItMatters: With antibiotic resistance rising, bacteriophages offer an alternative treatment for infections that no longer respond to drugs. Phage therapy has already saved patients with untreatable infections when all antibiotics failed.
takeaways: Phages outnumber bacteria roughly 10 to 1 in most environments
Each phage species targets specific bacterial species with high precision
Phage therapy has successfully treated antibiotic-resistant infections in humans

faq.question: How do bacteriophages kill bacteria?
faq.answer: A phage attaches to a specific receptor on the bacterial surface, injects its DNA, hijacks the cell's machinery to produce hundreds of new phages, then bursts the bacterium open to release them. This lytic cycle destroys the host cell completely.

faq.question: Why is phage therapy not more widely used?
faq.answer: Phage specificity means each infection requires matching the right phage to the bacterial strain. Regulatory frameworks were designed for chemical drugs, not living biological agents. The success of antibiotics overshadowed phage research in the West for decades.
